These exercises use the same CTM question controls as the [backend comparison](examples.qmd).
Question variables, supported input validation and native response-tree nodes run through
STACK's Maxima libraries in WebAssembly. Native questions start without Python. A visited
PythonChecker node loads the existing CTM checker implementation in Pyodide and then resumes
the native response tree.

The supported controller subset is explicit; this page does not establish full Moodle PHP
input-controller or attempt-state compatibility. Use **Run question tests** where available,
then try your own correct, incorrect and invalid answers. Source XML links identify the
exact questions used by this build.

## Rational equivalence

**Standard STACK features; CTM-authored question.** This checks the same mathematical
condition as the comparison page. The selected variants are prepared by native Maxima.
[Source XML](native-questions/native-rational.xml).

#| prepared: native-rational

## An unchanged upstream binding example

**Unchanged upstream STACK question.** The board is rendered by the existing
`jsxgraph-quarto` extension, with STACK's own point-binding library and a CTM input adapter.
The upstream prose describes Moodle's reload behavior; this static page keeps the board
mounted while checking. **This teaching example compares the input with itself, so any
valid answer receives full credit. It demonstrates data exchange, not mathematical grading.**
[Source XML](native-questions/native-binding.xml).

::: {.stack-native #native-binding}
#| prepared: native-binding
:::

## An unchanged upstream JSON example

**Unchanged upstream STACK question.** Its original input is a **string** containing JSON.
Native `stackjson_parse` reads that string and the feedback reports the number and colors
of the points. Drag the black source point out of its circle to create a point in the
answer, then move it through the colored circles. **Its grading also compares the input
with itself.** [Source XML](native-questions/native-json.xml).

::: {.stack-native #native-json}
#| prepared: native-json
:::

## A graphical PythonChecker

**CTM extension: PythonChecker. This question does not run on vanilla STACK.** The board
exchanges the same coordinate-list response as an ordinary STACK binding. The existing
PythonChecker API decides whether both coordinates are positive.
Switch variants to see a different initial point; the accepted condition stays the same.
Typing in the bound input moves the point; the board writes back its resulting coordinate pair.
[Source XML](native-questions/native-python-board.xml) · [Checker source](native-questions/native-checkers.py).

::: {.stack-native #native-python-board}
#| prepared: native-python-board
:::

## A mixed response tree

**CTM extension: PythonChecker inside a native response tree. This question does not run on
vanilla STACK.** Three nodes run in the order **native → Python → native**. Try `[2,2]`
for full credit, `[2,3]` for half credit and `[-1,3]` for zero. The native continuation
retains the branch path and score when the Python node finishes.
The feedback displays the same target before and after the Python node.
[Source XML](native-questions/native-mixed-board.xml).

::: {.stack-native #native-mixed-board}
#| prepared: native-mixed-board
:::

## Structured matrix feedback from PythonChecker

**CTM extension: PythonChecker matrix assessment. This question does not run on vanilla
STACK.** The checker returns a verdict for each submitted column. Those verdicts explain
the result; the response tree awards the score. Try the identity matrix and then change
one entry in its second column. [Source XML](native-questions/native-matrix-python.xml).

::: {.stack-native #native-matrix-python}
#| prepared: native-matrix-python
:::

## Public startup and response times {#public-startup-and-response-times}

**The native worker starts on the first Validate; Python stays unloaded until a visited
PythonChecker node needs it.** First native Validate took a median **38.72 s**, including
**38.60 s** of native initialization. Warm native Validate took **104 ms**, and warm
native Check took **336 ms**. On an already initialized native worker, the first
graphical PythonChecker Check added **6.13 s** of UI time, including **5.80 s** of Python
startup; subsequent Checks took **332 ms**.

These frozen measurements describe deployed source
**`15fa33299d68d64e122a2661a2868feb30130edb`**, measured on **22 October 2026** by
[benchmark attempt 2](https://github.com/Erasmus-CTM/stack-wasm-maxima/actions/runs/39831459804/attempts/2). Later documentation builds do not remeasure this batch.
The native workload uses the first variant of the rational question and its prepared
model answer. The graphical workload uses the first PythonChecker board and `[2,2]`.

Values are **median / minimum / maximum**. First operations and board validation have
**3 samples**; warm rows have **15 samples**, five calls in each of three fresh processes.
The unit is shown per row.

| Actual button operation | UI: click to verdict | Worker RPC |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Native first Validate (s) | 38.716 / 38.514 / 40.782 | 0.115 / 0.112 / 0.115 |
| Native warm Validate (ms) | 103.89 / 100.07 / 111.05 | 102.81 / 99.07 / 109.93 |
| Native first Check after validation (ms) | 418.16 / 413.02 / 422.33 | 416.86 / 411.71 / 420.84 |
| Native warm Check (ms) | 335.71 / 328.75 / 408.71 | 334.61 / 327.83 / 407.71 |
| Board Validate before Python (ms) | 2180.66 / 1697.03 / 2223.28 | 1376.68 / 1081.51 / 1420.63 |
| First PythonChecker Check (s) | 6.128 / 6.041 / 6.238 | 6.109 / 6.020 / 6.217 |
| Warm PythonChecker Check (ms) | 331.67 / 325.13 / 402.90 | 312.11 / 305.72 / 382.99 |

Native initialization alone was **38.600 / 38.400 / 40.665 s** (3 samples).
Optional Python initialization alone was **5.798 / 5.705 / 5.897 s** (3 samples).
They are included in the relevant first UI operations; do not add the rows together.
The first native Validate worker RPC excludes the separately measured initialization.
First PythonChecker Check reuses warm Maxima, so it measures incremental Python startup,
not a second cold page. Board Validate is native-only and includes the real graphical
collection/replay gate; its UI interval includes that gate as well as the worker call.

Each profile began with zero assessment RPCs, created one native worker and made
**20 real RPCs**; six grades visited a **PythonChecker callback**. All three profiles recorded
zero interpreter/stdlib/wheel requests and `pythonLoaded=false` through board validation;
the first Python grade then loaded Python exactly once. The shared small
`pyodide-runtime.js` configuration helper is not counted as an interpreter download.

UI time starts at the original click, before graphical collection, and ends at the
verdict DOM update. Worker RPC time is the actual message/response interval. Page
navigation, HTML loading, isolation setup, answer entry and later MathJax painting are
excluded. Chromium **141.0.7390.37** ran on one GitHub-hosted Ubuntu runner
with **4 virtual CPUs**, using three fresh browser processes/profiles.
OS and CDN caches were not cleared; provenance requests can warm CDN caches.

The browser's final service-worker Document response was exactly **16,855,012 bytes**
with the expected HTML hash in every profile. HTML and public runtime/frontend asset
hashes also matched before and after the batch. The
[summary evidence](https://github.com/Erasmus-CTM/stack-wasm-maxima/tree/research/2026-10-native-stack/reports/milestone-three/timings/39831459804-attempt-2/) retains those actual navigation hashes, sample numbers,
worker/callback counts, method and artifact provenance without copying question bodies.

This full native validation/response-tree path has higher warm costs than
[the hybrid comparison](examples.qmd#startup-and-response-times), which delegates only
ordinary answer-test nodes to Maxima. These two accepted-answer workloads on one runner
do not establish a general speed ranking or a controlled speedup over earlier builds.
Functional builds leave the measurements frozen.

## Build and execution evidence

### Supported subset

The native controller accepts algebraic, numerical and matrix inputs, plus string and
JSON inputs transported as quoted strings. Mathematical input uses the pinned
STACK-MP-lite recognizer and STACK security data, a bounded expression/function allowlist,
`strictsyntax=1` and `insertstars=0` or `1`. It preserves written forms for native tests
such as `LowestTerms` and decimal-place checks. Native STACK performs type and lowest-terms
validation; admission also handles `forbidfloat` and explicit `forbidwords`.

Learner assignments, indexing, statements and arbitrary function calls are unsupported.
So are `allowwords`, forbidden-word shorthand lists and other corrective-input modes.
The [input implementation](https://github.com/Erasmus-CTM/stack-wasm-maxima/blob/research/2026-10-native-stack/prototype/native/input.js)
defines the exact function list and size/depth limits.

Question variables use top-level assignments, with prepared values and model answers
frozen for each seed. Nested assignments, state-mutating author calls and random
response-tree/feedback expressions are outside this subset. Feedback variables cannot
reassign learner inputs. Authors remain trusted; these checks define supported state
behavior, not an author-code sandbox. Boards belong to the prepared question and cannot
be created by feedback.

The feedback adapter displays 63 selected English messages from the pinned STACK source.
Unknown or unsupported protocols remain visible as escaped, labelled raw feedback.
This is bounded translation, not Moodle's complete feedback interpreter.

The [native build manifest](../native/build-manifest.json) records the pinned source
revisions, original XML hashes, actual native preparation programs and prepared variants.
Browser CI exercises the controls, the JSON bridge, native and Python routing, partial
credit, reset and question independence. Loading measurements are reported separately
from ordinary functional builds.

The reference report records desktop and Wasm Maxima versions separately. Scores,
branch state, answer notes and canonical answer sources are compared strictly (finite
floating-point values use a stated tolerance). Raw display output is retained. Two
narrowly defined TeX differences between core versions are reported separately:
equivalent text-box wrappers with identical content, and math-only line wrapping.
Those presentation differences do not stand in for agreement on grading.

### Historical controlled loader measurements

The loader now fetches one verified package of the original runtime library files.
A controlled comparison used three fresh Chromium processes per condition and loader,
then ran a real native answer test in every sample:

| Local server condition | Original native readiness, median | Bundled readiness, median | HTTP requests |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| No added latency | 38.57 s | 36.71 s | 137 → 12 |
| Simulated 80 ms per request | 48.32 s | 37.39 s | 137 → 12 |

These are **local loader measurements**, including an explicitly simulated latency,
from [run 39802432330](https://github.com/Erasmus-CTM/stack-wasm-maxima/actions/runs/39802432330).
They measure native readiness, not button-to-verdict time on this public page.
[Raw reports and exact source hashes](https://github.com/Erasmus-CTM/stack-wasm-maxima/tree/research/2026-10-native-stack/reports/milestone-three/loading)
keep the experiment reproducible. First validation on this native page still needs
the native runtime; a PythonChecker adds its own lazy startup when its node is reached.
Ordinary site builds run functional checks and leave these benchmark statistics frozen.
